newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 28.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Friday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Investors put a record $29.39 billion into stock mutual funds in January, and executives say they expect February to be another strong month.
* The Justice Department is close to clearing Bell Atlantic's purchase of NYNEX, but a fight over compensation for customers is delaying approval from New York state.
* Carl Icahn sold his 7.3 percent interest in RJR Nabisco for mroe than $730 million, giving up his proxy battle against the company.
* Ford is suspending its Thunderbird and does not plan to introduce a new version of the 42-year-old brand until after the year 2000.

* The Federal Trade Commission fined Germany's Mahle Gmbh autoparts maker and Brazil's Metal Leve SA $5.1 million for failing to give federal antitrust regulators advance notice of their planned merger.
* The $3.5 billion merger between Staples and Office Depot goes today before Federal antitrust regulators, who may consider blocking the deal.
* American Express named Kenneth Chenault president and chief operating officer, making him the official heir-apparent to Chairman and Chief Executive Havey Golub.
* Technology stocks fell, sending the Nasdaq composite down 27.89 to 1,312.66. The Dow industrials fell 58.11 to 6,925.07. Bond prices and the dollar also fell.
* Texas Pacific Group, a buyout firm, has agreed to acquire Del Monte Foods.
* Aetna is expected to make the co-president of its health care unit, Joseph Sebastianelli, either its president or vice-chairman.
* Time Warner has ordered budget cuts of three to five percent over the next three years, according to people familiar with the deal.
* A federal judge dismissed San Francisco's lawsuit to recover public health costs from the tobacco industry.
* The U.S. Internal Revenue Service banned a tax-advanted corporate security known as step-down preferred stock, cancelling billions of dollars in planned deals.

* Alan Greenspan seems to think investors aren't worrying enough about stock market risk these days. But some Wall Street experts say Mr. Greenspan may be worrying too much about the risks. -- Heard on the Street.

* Sellers again dominated the bond market but decines were modest, despite new evidence of strength in the economy and continuing concern the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates. -- Credit Markets.
